You sometimes use one verb after another verb.

Often the second verb is in the infinitive form which is the base form of a verb (to+verb).
For example:
  • I want to know what you think of this story.

Sometimes the second verb must be in gerund form, for example:
  • One resourceful man suggested asking Mari for help.
Knowing when to use a gerund depends on the first verb. Some verbs can only be followed by a gerund.

A gerund is used after some phrasal verbs.
A phrasal verb is a verb+preposition or adverb.
For example:
  • give up: Ricardo gave up smoking.

There are some phrasal verbs that include the word "to" as a preposition.
For example: look forward to. In these cases, a gerund after the phrasal verb is needed since to (in this case) is a preposition and NOT part of the infinitive form.
For example:
  • I look forward to meeting you.
 Other phrasal verbs include: carry on, give up, leave off, put off.

Gerunds are also used after some expressions.
For example:
  • I can't stand losing you.
 Other expressions include: can't help, can't stand, be worth, It's no use.
When you choose to use the passive voice, you choose to change the focus of what you are writing or saying.
You use the passive voice to focus the reader's or listener's attention to the receiver of the action.
Miguel and Ignacio hated being sent to bed.
In this case, the interest is not in who sent them to bed, but the fact that they don't like going to bed.
They loved being told stories about the myths and legends of their ancestors.
Again, here the focus is on who receives the action, not on who does the action.
They enjoyed being reminded of the ancient Basque tales.
They appreciated being lulled to sleep by grandfather's voice.
They were being carried into the land of dreams.

images.text:
Miguel and Ignacio hated being sent to bed. They wanted to stay up when their grandfather was visiting. They loved being told stories about the myths and legends of their ancestors. They enjoyed being reminded of the ancient Basque tales. They appreciated being lulled to sleep by grandfather's voice.
Grandfather Bernardo smiled to himself. He remembered his grandfather telling him the old stories when he was a child. “All right boys, get into your warm bed,” he began, “be quiet, close your eyes and listen.”

"A magical lady called Mari has lived in the Basque mountain caves since time began. While she's in the caves, Mari enjoys changing shape. Imagine her appearing as a goat or a snake or bear! She loves becoming these animals and exploring the deep dark recesses of the mountain.
She does not always stay inside the mountain. Leaving the caves involves Mari turning into a golden-haired woman draped in crimson and gold. She shines like fire as she keeps moving across the sky. She blazes through the day, lighting the world. Then, when she returns to her cave, there is darkness.

The ancient Basques were frightened by the monsters and spirits that came from the bowels of the earth when the skies grew dark. One resourceful man suggested asking Mari for help. Mari agreed. She created a bright being to walk through the dark firmament at night for them. Mari called her ‘Moon'.”
Bernardo looked down at his grandchildren. They were being carried into the land of dreams . He kissed his grandchildren and tucked them in. He hoped retelling the legends would be part of the Basque future.
